--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.shortest_path()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Find shortest path between two nodes. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.shortest_path()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Find shortest path between two nodes. title: >- [Graph.shortest_path()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Find shortest path between two nodes. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find shortest path between two nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L59949-L60122){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.shortest_path( source, target, attr_name=None, return_list=False, weighted=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Shortest path (fewest hops)](../assets/graphs/shortest-path.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The same directed weighted graph with three routes from A to F. shortest_path runs a breadth-first search, so it ignores the weights and returns the two-hop path A, D, F in the accent color, with filled badges giving each node's position 0, 1, 2." width="100%"} Finds a single shortest route from `source=` to `target=`. The meaning of "shortest" depends on how the graph was created, unless `weighted=` overrides it: - for an unweighted graph (the default, `Graph(weighted=False)`), a breadth-first search (BFS) finds the path with the fewest hops, and any edge weights are ignored - for a weighted graph (`Graph(weighted=True)`), Dijkstra's algorithm finds the path with the lowest total edge weight; edges without a weight count as `1.0` In directed graphs, the path follows edge directions. If several paths are equally short, one of them is returned. Can return the path as a list, or store the position of each node along the path as a node attribute for visualization. Shortest paths are a basic building block for routing and navigation, tracing how two entities are connected (for example, the chain of contacts between two people), and highlighting a route in a plot. Dijkstra's algorithm assumes non-negative weights; if your graph has negative weights, use `bellman_ford_shortest_path()` instead. For heuristic or anytime search, see `ada_star_search()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Node where the path starts, given as an integer node ID or a string label. An ID or label that isn't in the graph raises a `NodeNotFoundError` (a `ValueError`). [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Node where the path ends, given as an integer node ID or a string label, with the same rules as `source=`. If `target=` equals `source=`, the path is just that node. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node attribute to store path position. If `None`, uses `shortest_path_order` as the attribute name. Only nodes on the path get this attribute set; positions are 0-based (`source=` is `0`), and all other nodes get a null value. Use a different name for each call to keep several paths side by side. Only used when `return_list=` is `False`. [return_list]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns list of node IDs in the path and leaves the node DataFrame untouched. If `False` (default), stores positions as node attributes under `attr_name=` and returns self for chaining. [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to measure paths by edge weight or by number of hops. If `None` (default), follows the graph: weights are used on a weighted graph (`Graph(weighted=True)`) and ignored otherwise. Pass `False` for the path with the fewest hops on a weighted graph, or `True` to use the weights of an unweighted one. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[list[int], Graph, None]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_list=` is `True`: list of node IDs from source to target (inclusive), or `None` if no path exists. If `return_list=` is `False` it returns self for method chaining, or `None` if no path exists. Because of the latter, a chain such as `graph.shortest_path(...).plot()` fails when the target is unreachable. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `source=` or `target=` is an ID or label that does not exist in the graph. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~shortest_path_length`) : The distance alone, without the path. [](`~all_shortest_paths`) : Every path that ties for shortest. [](`~k_shortest_paths`) : The shortest path, the next shortest, and so on. [](`~astar_path`) : A shortest path found with a distance estimate to guide the search. [](`~bellman_ford_shortest_path`) : Shortest paths with negative edge weights. ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a weighted graph the route with the lowest total weight wins: A, B, C, F costs 4, while the shorter-looking route through D costs 6. `return_list=True` gives the node IDs along it: ::: {#19e4909d .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("A", "B", 1), ("B", "C", 2), ("C", "F", 1), ("A", "D", 3), ("D", "F", 3)], directed=True, ) graph.shortest_path("A", "F", return_list=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [1, 2, 3, 4] ``` ::: ::: Without it, each node on the path gets its position in the `shortest_path_order` column, and every other node gets a null: ::: {#eaaebaec .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.shortest_path("A", "F").get_node_df().select("label", "shortest_path_order") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
shape: (5, 2)

"A"0
"B"1
"C"2
"F"3
"D"null
``` ::: ::: ### Fastest isn't fewest stops The metro network is weighted by travel time, so its shortest path is the fastest route. `weighted=False` counts stops instead. From Westgate to Lakeside, the two disagree: ::: {#9d4e3b9f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} metro = ec.metro() ( metro.shortest_path_length("Westgate", "Lakeside"), metro.shortest_path_length("Westgate", "Lakeside", weighted=False), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (18.0, 4) ``` ::: ::: The fastest route takes 18 minutes and the one with the fewest stops takes 4 stops. Drawing each on the map shows why: the fastest route (left) goes through downtown on the Red line, 6 stops in all, while the fewest stops (right) take the Green line around the north side, which is slower at 22 minutes: ::: {layout-ncol="2"} ::: {#5691a97b .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} metro.shortest_path("Westgate", "Lakeside", attr_name="fastest") metro.plot( layout="pos", highlight="fastest", label_by="label", width=340, height=300, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {#6780bae8 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} metro.shortest_path("Westgate", "Lakeside", attr_name="fewest", weighted=False) metro.plot( layout="pos", highlight="fewest", label_by="label", width=340, height=300, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: Which is better depends on what a stop costs the traveler. For the next-best routes, use `k_shortest_paths()`, and when several routes tie for shortest, `all_shortest_paths()` lists them all. On a large map, `astar_path()` finds the same route faster with a distance estimate to steer it.
